name: Tarui disease (glycogen storage disease type VII)

reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive glycogenosis caused by deficiency of the muscle isoform of phosphofructokinase (PFKM gene), a key regulatory glycolytic enzyme
Presents like McArdle disease with exercise intolerance, cramps, and exertional muscle pain, but symptoms are often worse after a carbohydrate-rich meal
A carbohydrate load does not improve and may worsen exertional symptoms (the 'out of wind' effect), unlike the fuel benefit seen in some other glycogenoses
Because the enzyme is also partially deficient in red cells, a compensated haemolytic anaemia with reticulocytosis and hyperuricaemia frequently coexists
The forearm exercise test shows a flat lactate response, similar to McArdle disease
Exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria can occur, and some patients develop gout from the associated hyperuricaemia
Management is supportive with avoidance of intense exertion and, in contrast to some other glycogenoses, avoidance of high-carbohydrate pre-exercise loading
reference.pathophysiology: Tarui disease is caused by deficiency of the muscle subunit of phosphofructokinase, which catalyses the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, a committed and rate-limiting step of glycolysis. The block prevents muscle from using both stored glycogen and blood glucose for anaerobic energy production, so exercise capacity is limited and lactate fails to rise with exertion. Because ingested glucose cannot be utilised and instead suppresses the alternative free-fatty-acid fuel supply, a carbohydrate meal can paradoxically worsen exercise tolerance. The muscle-type PFK subunit is also expressed in erythrocytes, so its deficiency reduces red-cell glycolysis and causes a compensated haemolysis, with increased purine turnover contributing to hyperuricaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Other distal glycolytic enzyme defects (e.g. phosphoglycerate kinase or mutase deficiency)
additionalInvestigations: Forearm exercise test showing a flat lactate response
Full blood count and reticulocyte count for compensated haemolysis
Creatine kinase at rest and after exertion, with urine myoglobin during episodes
Molecular genetic testing of the PFKM gene
Muscle biopsy with phosphofructokinase enzyme assay
redFlags: Severe exertional rhabdomyolysis with pigmenturia and risk of acute kidney injury
Gout or urate nephropathy from hyperuricaemia
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a normal life expectancy with lifestyle adaptation, though exercise capacity is limited; recurrent rhabdomyolysis, complications of haemolysis, and gout are the main long-term concerns, and rare infantile-onset forms carry a poorer prognosis.
pitfalls: Advising carbohydrate loading before exercise, which can worsen symptoms in this glycogenosis
Confusing it with McArdle disease and missing the associated haemolysis and hyperuricaemia
Overlooking gout or urate nephropathy as a complication
Failing to counsel about rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury risk during strenuous activity
references: Scriver's The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Advise avoidance of strenuous and high-intensity exercise to prevent cramps and exertional rhabdomyolysis
Counsel against pre-exercise carbohydrate loading, which worsens exertional tolerance in the out-of-wind effect, unlike in McArdle disease
Consider a high-protein or ketogenic dietary approach to provide alternative muscle fuel
Manage acute exertional rhabdomyolysis with generous hydration and monitoring for acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia
Treat associated hyperuricaemia and gout with urate-lowering therapy such as allopurinol
Monitor the compensated haemolytic anaemia and reticulocytosis with periodic blood counts
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder with carrier testing of relatives
